transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-09
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Ramirez (Redwood); Aisha Patel, Tom Granger, Lena Zhou, Markus Lee (Cobalt AI)

Summary: Quick demo of org/project key patterns for multi-tenant rate controls (what we call fairburst internally), discussion of pilot parameters, security questions around private network and KMS. Agreed to run a short concurrency benchmark and share pilot SOW/pricing.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm maya, AE on the account, and diego will run through the demo. um quick round robin? could you say name and role?
[00:12] Aisha (Cobalt): hey it's aisha, head of platform. we own the inference gateways and the tenancy mapping.
[00:16] Tom (Cobalt): tom here, s-r-e. i'll run the benchmarks on our side.
[00:20] Lena (Cobalt): lena, product. i'm looking at how throttling will affect UX.
[00:25] Markus (Cobalt): markus from security, quick questions on encryption and logs.
[00:30] Diego (Redwood SE): great, thanks. real quick agenda: show org/project key routing patterns, fairburst behavior (burst allowances + steady quotas), console examples, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:42] Maya (Redwood AE): yeah and just to set context: Cobalt mentioned you run multi-tenant workloads with spikes from the UI and nightly batch. goal is predictable cost and stable latency while preserving per-tenant fairness. is that still right?
[00:55] Aisha: yes, exactly. spikes from interactive sessions matter more than batch, batch can be delayed. cost is a big one, we want to avoid overprovisioning.
[01:05] Diego: okay cool. i want to show two patterns: first org-first where org keys map to big quota pools and projects inherit, second project-first where individual project keys get explicit quotas and can burst. fairburst is our term for giving short bursts to projects up to a burst window then falling back to steady quotas.
[01:25] Diego: starting demo... i'm sharing my screen, console view. apologies if the naming is a little off, sometimes the auto transcriber writes red wood as two words, but you get it.
[01:40] [Screen: Redwood Console - Routing & Quotas]
[01:44] Diego: here's an org called cobalt-prod. you can see top-level org quota: tokens-per-minute and concurrency cap. under that we have projects: web-frontend, batch-tasks, partner-api. each project can override or be pinned to the org pool.
[02:05] Lena: can we set a project to have guaranteed throughput but lower burst? say web-frontend needs 200 rps steady but low burst.
[02:14] Diego: yes, you tune steady vs burst. there are two knobs: steady_quota and burst_window/burst_rate. steady_quota enforces long term rate, burst_window is short window smoothing. if a project exceeds burst allowance, requests will be rate-limited or routed to a cheaper model variant.
[02:32] Tom: quick question: if we hit org cap, can high-priority projects preempt tokens?
[02:37] Maya: yep we have priority tiers. you can set priority labels and the router will do weighted fairshare, and also preempt if higher tier critical requests arrive. it's configurable per org.
[02:47] Markus: how do audit logs look? we need per-token metadata for compliance — who called, which key, model, prompt hash for dedup checks.
[02:57] Diego: we stream audit events to your SIEM and include key id, project id, route, and model id. note: sometimes small fields like KV cache id might be munged in logs by the transcriber, but in production logs it's full fidelity.
[03:12] [03:12] Diego: switching to API examples — here's a request with org_key header and project_key header, both optional but recommended. if only org_key present, project is inferred and gets default project mapping.
[03:30] Diego: code sample: curl -H \"X-Redwood-Org: cobalt-prod\" -H \"X-Redwood-Project: web-frontend\" ... then you can pass route param to select latency-tier model.
[03:46] Lena: and how sticky is routing if we fail over to a fallback model? will cookies or keys preserve session?
[03:52] Diego: sessions rely on project_key + session_id to keep KV cache affinity. fallbacks are per-request but we try to maintain affinity by routing back to same model when capacity returns. occasionally the KV cache name is different and you'll see a cold start, which is expected.
[04:10] Aisha: tell us more about fairburst — does the burst allowance reset instantly?
[04:14] Diego: it's a leaky-bucket style. burst credits accumulate up to a cap, and you can configure refill rate. default is small so short interactive spikes get served, long sustained load consumes steady quota.
[04:26] Tom: can we cap burst per minute at org-level while allowing project-level bursts? we want to avoid noisy neighbors hogging whole org burst.
[04:33] Maya: yes, you can set org-level burst ceiling and also per-project guaranteed reservations. router enforces org ceiling first then project-level fairness.
[04:42] [05:00] Dieg0 (transcript typo): sorry, small typo there — the console shows concurrency limit in slots (we call them worker slots) and token rate in tps but some labels may be different in your console depending on feature flags.
[05:12] Markus: for private deployments, we require KMS integration with our HSM. is that supported?
[05:18] Diego: absolutely. for Redwood Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; keys never leave your control plane. note that on prem deploys may have slightly different kernel selection and quantization settings which can change latency numbers.
[05:34] Lena: about observability — can we see per-project cost and token breakdown?
[05:39] Maya: yes, in Optimize and Console you get token-level cost breakdown, model breakdown, and per-route traces. you can export CSVs for billing.
[05:50] Aisha: our security team will want SOC2 artifacts and network diagrams.
[05:54] Maya: we'll attach SOC2 summary and a network diagram showing egress IPs — action item for us.
[06:02] [06:20] Diego: now running through a live scenario: 10 projects have steady quotas, one project suddenly spikes 10x for 2 minutes. here's how fairburst behaves — project will consume burst credits up to its per-project cap, then router enforces fallback: either queue, throttle or route to a cheaper/generic model.
[06:40] Diego: i'll flip to the routing policy page to show fallback policies. you can set per-route fallback to lower-cost model, circuit-break to deny, or enqueue for a short time.
[06:52] Tom: if we enqueue, what's the max wait window? we should avoid user-facing timeouts > 5s ideally.
[06:58] Diego: you can set max_queue_ms, default 3000 ms, but it's configurable per-route. the router honors latency SLOs and will drop to fallback if queue would exceed threshold.
[07:12] Lena: thinking about product: if model falls back to cheaper variant, will output quality degrade noticeably for chat flows?
[07:19] Diego: yes potentially; Optimize provides profiles so you can run small evals to see degradation on your prompt set. we also support automatic A/B rollouts so you can test fallback on a subset.
[07:32] Aisha: could the fallback be to an on-prem model in our network? we have a small local model for basic responses.
[07:39] Maya: with Redwood Private you can hybrid route: host an on-prem lightweight model and route non-critical requests there while critical ones go to hosted Redwood. there is a routing policy for home-region first.
[07:52] Markus: logging and retention — we need 7 years for certain audit trails, is that configurable?
[07:58] Diego: retention is configurable; long-term retention is an add-on plan. you'll get immutable audit logs and export hooks to your archive.
[08:10] [08:20] Diego: quick note about token accounting: due to tokenization differences between models you might see slight variance in reported token counts; we normalize and show per-model breakdown. sometimes transcripts refer to K-V cache as K V cash in the logs, just a transcriber oddity.
[08:34] Tom: regarding quota enforcement, do we get webhooks when a project hits 80% of quota?
[08:39] Maya: yes, you can hook to webhooks or our events bus and trigger alerts. we also emit granular metrics to prometheus / datadog.
[08:51] Lena: for the pilot, what's the minimum committed capacity?
[08:55] Maya: pilot can be done on hosted with a small reserved pool — you can do a 30k token/min reservation for the first month to get stable metrics. dedicated reserved capacity starts higher and is negotiated.
[09:08] Aisha: we probably want hosted pilot first to validate configs before any private deployment.
[09:12] Maya: totally makes sense. hosted pilot + IP allowlist to restrict access.
[09:20] [09:35] Diego: switching back to console to show the project mapping UI: you can bulk-upload CSV with project ids, owner emails, steady/burst quotas, priority tiers. i often recommend setting low steady and small burst to start.
[09:55] Diego: also showing auto-scaling policies for dedicated pools — capacity can autoscale on metrics like queue depth and token consumption with soft and hard limits.
[10:08] Tom: curious about billing: if a project eats burst from the org pool, how is cost attributed?
[10:14] Maya: cost attribution can be per-project or org-level depending on tagging. we recommend per-project billing for visibility; you can set sticky routing to ensure tokens are charged to the right project. exports include token counts and model ids.
[10:30] Lena: any gotchas for sessionized chat where KV cache matters?
[10:34] Diego: cold starts will affect latency and cost, and you should pin long-running sessions to a project affinity key to keep the KV cache hot. also consider cache pre-warming for large cohorts.
[10:47] Aisha: does Redwood Optimize recommend specific quantization or batching settings per workload?
[10:52] Diego: yes optimize will scan traffic patterns and recommend batch sizes, quantization profiles and which model variants are cost effective. it will also simulate cost impact.
[11:05] [11:20] Maya: okay let's move to the more technical Qs from markus.
[11:24] Markus: encryption in transit and at rest — we need TLS mTLS between our gateways and your endpoints and customer-managed keys for at-rest encryption.
[11:33] Diego: we support mTLS and customer KMS. for hosted there's a managed KMS option but enterprise/private supports HSM-backed keys. for on-prem we can integrate with your HSM via standard KMIP or cloud KMS connectors.
[11:48] Markus: great. second, do request-level logs include raw prompt text? some teams require prompt redaction.
[11:54] Maya: you can configure retention and redaction policies — prompt hashing is supported and raw prompts can be omitted from logs.
[12:03] Tom: question on throttling: what's the worst-case latency when rate-limited and we choose to queue vs reject?
[12:09] Diego: queue adds a few hundred ms up to your max_queue_ms. reject returns 429 quickly. we also provide an adaptive token bucket so most requests either go through or are fast-failed.
[12:22] Lena: do you have tenant-level SLOs for latency?
[12:26] Maya: we have tiered SLOs in SLAs. hosted real-time tiers target p95 under X ms depending on model and region. we'll share SLO tables in the follow-up.
[12:37] [12:50] Diego: demo time: i'm going to simulate a spike from web-frontend. watching the console: project consumes burst, then hits per-project cap, then org ceiling starts to enforce and lower-priority projects are throttled. you can see metrics on the right.
[13:12] Aisha: can we tune the preemption so partner-api is never dropped?
[13:16] Diego: set partner-api to critical priority and reserve guaranteed tokens; that reservation sits outside the org burst pool so it won't be preempted.
[13:27] Markus: in the pilot we need ability to audit configuration changes. is there RBAC and change history?
[13:33] Maya: yes RBAC with role tiers, SSO/SAML integration, and an audit trail showing who changed quotas, when, and the old value.
[13:44] Tom: for the benchmark, Diego, what do you need from us?
[13:47] Diego: sample traffic profile (rps distribution, payload sizes), representative prompt sets, and a target latency SLO. we'll provide a load runner script and expected metrics.
[13:58] Aisha: we'll send that by 2026-01-14.
[14:02] Maya: great.
[14:10] [14:20] Diego: quick aside: we also support sticky API keys for per-user quotas within a project, useful if you sell per-seat.
[14:28] Lena: that's helpful.
[14:32] Diego: moving on: config as code — all quota configs can be templated and applied via our API, so you can automate tenant onboarding.
[14:42] Markus: can we also version configs and roll back?
[14:46] Diego: yes, configs are versioned and can be rolled back with canary release options.
[14:53] [15:00] Maya: ok real quick pricing note — for pilot hosted pricing is usage plus a small fixed pilot fee. i'll send the tiered pricing sheet.
[15:08] Aisha: what's the overage policy if we exceed pilot reservation?
[15:12] Maya: overage billed at on-demand rates; we'll flag you at 80% utilization automatically.
[15:19] Tom: about the concurrency quota pattern you've recommended in other calls, can we combine concurrency slots with token quotas?
[15:26] Diego: yes, a hybrid model is common: concurrency slots control model instantiation and memory pressure while token quotas control sustained throughput. using both gives you fine-grained control.
[15:39] Lena: any edge-case where this breaks?
[15:42] Diego: if you have very spiky short requests with large tokens, you may need to tune both and consider request batching or pre-emptive splitting.
[15:53] [16:05] Maya: all right let's surface the key decisions and next steps: pilot on hosted, provide sample traffic, Diego will run benchmark checklist, Maya sends SOW + pricing + SOC2 + network diagram.
[16:18] Aisha: sounds good. quick security question: will logs with prompt hashes be exportable to our SIEM without raw text?
[16:25] Diego: yes, export with hashed prompts and all metadata.
[16:30] Markus: and you support IP allowlist and SSO?
[16:33] Maya: yes to both.
[16:36] Tom: for the benchmark window, we want a 2-hour run at peak sim and a 24-hour soak for steady state; is that feasible?
[16:44] Diego: yes we can run both, we'll coordinate scope with you.
[16:48] [17:00] Maya: any final Qs?
[17:04] Lena: no final Qs from product, we're good with pilot scope.
[17:06] Aisha: none here, thanks.
[17:08] Markus: one more on data residency — our EU tenants must keep logs in EU region. is region-scoped retention possible?
[17:14] Diego: yes, retention and storage can be region-scoped for logs and backups. we'll detail in follow-up.
[17:26] Maya: perfect. thanks everyone. recap of owners in calendar invite and we'll follow up with docs.
